problems: Minor (non-blocking): the .md says the password row has 'no visible text' — accurate, but worth noting the failure depends on the password input being empty/unfocused; if a UA were to render a value, the border ceases to be the sole cue. The resting empty state is the SC-relevant state, so the label is correct.

Minor (non-blocking): the failure is contingent on the .sr-only label genuinely removing the visible word 'Password'; confirmed the clip-rect CSS does this and the AX tree still exposes textbox name='Password', so the name-vs-visual asymmetry the case relies on is real.

Minor citation-fit nuance (not a defect): the task's named citation is the 'Buttons' passing example ('A button which has a distinguishing indicator such as position, text style, or context...'), which is verbatim in wcag-understanding/non-text-contrast.html and from the correct document, but it speaks to buttons distinguished by position/text-style/context rather than directly to the icon-only failure. The on-point justification is the 'Boundaries' paragraph ('Having a visual boundary indicating the hit area is only required when there is no other visual way to identify the presence of the control - and in those cases, the boundary must have sufficient non-text contrast...'), which the .md also cites verbatim. So the failure rationale rests on a correctly-quoted, directly-applicable passage; the 'Buttons' quote is accurate supplemental context, not a misattribution.

Minor pedantic note (not disqualifying): the 2.38:1 border is non-zero contrast and thus faintly perceptible, and the field sits within a visible form layout; a strict reader could argue the box is not entirely without a visual cue. The SC text resolves this in the case's favor (when the boundary is the sole cue it must reach 3:1, which it does not), so the failed verdict stands.

The .sr-only label resolves as the accessible name (CDP AX: role=textbox, name='مبلغ آخر لمرة واحدة'), so this is correctly framed as a visual low-vision failure, NOT a programmatic-name failure — the doc states this accurately.

Minor (non-defect): unusual double-label pattern — a <label for="p-appt"> sits inside the aria-hidden .box AND another <label for="p-appt"> inside .text. The AX name still resolves correctly (Chromium exposes role=checkbox, name='Appointment reminders by SMS', checked=true) and there are no JS errors, so it does not affect the 1.4.11 verdict, but it is slightly atypical markup.

PROMPT-vs-PAGE MISMATCH (not a page defect, but flag it): the orchestration prompt's 'Claimed scenario' describes colors that do NOT exist in the HTML — thumb #C8C8C8 on rail #B0B0B0 at 1.30:1 and a green track #2E7D32 (~5.1:1). The actual page uses thumb #74B97A on green track #4E9E52, computed contrast 1.415:1, and green-track-vs-white-page 3.314:1. The prompt scenario is stale/wrong; the HTML+MD tell a consistent (different) story.

HTML inline comment inaccuracy: comments at lines 39, 57 and the .note at line 119 state thumb-vs-track is '1.32:1', but the real computed ratio is 1.415:1 (verified independently and via inspect.js effectiveAncestorBg=#74B97A over track #4E9E52). The MD doc correctly says 1.41. The discrepancy is cosmetic — 1.32 and 1.41 both fail 3:1 — but the HTML comment number is wrong.

MD Scenario line 4 says 'Four are in the ON state on load (one is OFF...)', implying five toggles; the HTML has only FOUR toggles total and the AX tree confirms exactly 3 ON + 1 OFF. The MD's later text ('the OFF switch', 'three are ON') is consistent with 3 ON/1 OFF, so line 4's 'Four ... ON' is an internal typo. The selector/title in the MD also waver between 1.41 and 'four'.

Minor doc overstatement (not a defect, no fix required): the .md/scenario calls the chevron 'the ONLY graphical cue' of open/closed, but the panel itself visibly opens/closes via the max-height transition (line 40), which is a secondary visual state cue. This does not undermine the failure — under 1.4.11 the chevron is the designated in-component state-indicator graphic and must itself meet 3:1 against its adjacent surface regardless of other cues — but the 'sole cue' framing is slightly stronger than the code supports.

Boundary note (informational): the chevron stroke #8A96A6 vs the white page is 3.00:1, exactly at threshold; this is the distractor surface and irrelevant since the correct adjacent surface is the band (effectiveAncestorBg=rgb(92,107,126)=#5C6B7E) giving 1.81:1. Confirms the failure is robust against the wrong comparison.

Minor (non-blocking, unrelated to SC under test): the listbox places tabindex=0 on all 6 options instead of the APG roving-tabindex pattern (one 0, rest -1 with arrow-key navigation). The inspect tabOrder shows all options Tab-focusable. This is a small pattern deviation and does not affect the 1.4.11 contrast mechanism.

Subtlety in the 'sole visual cue' framing (does NOT invalidate the case): selected rows 1 and 3 are odd rows whose natural zebra background is #FFFFFF but selection forces them to #EEF2F7, so there IS a background change. However that change makes selected odd rows blend into the surrounding even rows (also #EEF2F7), so background does not discriminate selected from unselected within the rendered list — the accent bar remains the only reliable cue, and it fails contrast. The mechanism holds.

Minor cosmetic only: HTML/MD state the glow-vs-body ratio as 1.48:1 while the exact sRGB computation is 1.475:1 (the prompt header itself says 1.47:1). Pure rounding; far below 3:1 either way, no effect on outcome.

The filled-state mark is a 6x6px inner-glow circle (cx=12 cy=11 r=3.4) inside a 22px star; its adjacency surface is correctly the gold star body, but the tested element's small overlap area is something a tester must perceive geometrically — the inspect box (6x6) confirms it overlays the body, supporting the mechanism rather than refuting it.

Minor: the SVG carries role=img + aria-label (line 51-52), so the AX tree exposes a single labelled image and the four polylines have no individual a11y presence. The label is a topic-level description (not value-equivalent text), so it does not exempt the lines — the mechanism still holds, but the doc could note that the aria-label itself is also not the equivalent text exemption, not only the legend.
No substantive defects. The 'issue' is intentionally a Not-Applicable boundary case (severity=none reflects that the page correctly conforms, not that a barrier exists).

Minor/philosophical: label could arguably be 'passed' rather than 'inapplicable' since the graphical objects do exist and are merely exempted; but 'inapplicable' is defensible and consistent with sibling case-02, so not a defect.

Minor: the CSS-attribute selector svg.bubbles circle[fill="#DCE6F1"] passed to inspect.js resolves to only the first of five identically-filled circles (cx=100,r=62). The analysis still holds because all five bubbles share the same #DCE6F1 fill and all five icons share #B8CCE4, so the family-level mechanism is unaffected — but the selector is not unique.

Minor: the .md selector text says circles are ~1.26:1 'vs the white page' while the card surface is #fcfdfe (1.24:1). The SVG draws an explicit <rect fill=#ffffff> at line 52, so the circles do sit against true white — claim is accurate. No defect, noted for precision.

Minor SC-attribution nuance (not a defect, worth noting): the focus indicator itself has ~17:1 contrast against adjacent colors, so the literal 1.4.11 contrast-of-focus-state requirement (non-text-contrast.html line 45) technically passes. The actual defect is INDISTINGUISHABILITY (resting decoration == focus indicator), which is the F78 / 2.4.7 mechanism. Filing under 1.4.11 is still defensible because WCAG itself maps F78 to 1.4.11/2.4.7/2.4.13 (F78.html title) and there is a curated 6-case F78 cluster in this SC dir; the .md honestly labels it 'failed (SC 1.4.11, also implicates 2.4.7 / F78)'.
The 'failed' verdict is most precisely a 2.4.7 Focus Visible (F78) failure surfaced under 1.4.11; reviewers expecting a pure adjacent-color contrast deficiency should note the SC overlap.

Title/heading mismatch (cosmetic, not a verdict defect): the .md title (line 1) says the 4px border 'swallows the browser's default black focus outline', but the page does NOT use the UA default ring — it declares an EXPLICIT author outline (.btn:focus { outline: 2px solid #000 }). The body of the same .md (lines 5-16) and the HTML comment correctly state it is an author outline declared explicitly to defeat modern Chrome's accent-color default. The title line is internally contradictory but the mechanism described everywhere else is correct.

Faithful-reproduction caveat (not a defect, worth noting): the canonical F78 example is 'a {border: medium solid black}' with NO author outline, relying on the UA default ring. This page deliberately forces an explicit black author outline because modern Chrome paints the default ring in the accent color (blue), which would NOT be occluded. The deviation is necessary to reproduce F78(b) on a modern engine and is fully documented in both the HTML comment (lines 24-28) and .md (lines 13-16); it does not undermine the failure.

Minor: the doc states blue #2f6df6 on white is '~4:1'; actual ratio is ~3.7:1. Not load-bearing because the claimed failure is explicitly relational distinguishability, not a contrast-ratio shortfall, but the rounding is slightly generous.

Cosmetic (tool artifact, not a page defect): inspect.js reports the selector '.nav-item:focus' as 'selector not found' because pseudo-classes cannot be resolved via querySelector; the focused state was still correctly observed via the AX tree ('Funnels' focused:true) and computed styles.

Minor (non-blocking): the element-under-test selector `.seg:focus` is a dynamic pseudo-class and cannot be resolved by a static query — inspect.js returned 'selector not found' for it. The failure is real but only manifests with the focused-unselected element coexisting with the selected element (set up via autofocus); the selector is descriptive, not statically pinpointable.

Minor: doc estimates teal #0f8a8a-on-white at '~3.3:1'; actual computed contrast is 4.18:1 on the white card / 3.76:1 on the body bg. The conservative estimate does not change the conclusion (contrast is adequate; this is a state-distinguishability failure, not a contrast shortfall), but the number is imprecise.

Citation is labeled 'F78 (a/b hybrid)': the verbatim F78 example is about an element outline that mimics the FOCUS indicator; here the collision is FOCUS-indicator vs SELECTION-state indicator. This is a faithful, honestly-flagged extension rather than a literal F78 instance — acceptable, but the primary normative basis is 1.4.11/2.4.7 state distinguishability, supported by the second (also verbatim) Understanding 1.4.11 quote.

Minor citation-precision note (not a defect): the prompt's claimed citation (non-text-contrast.html lines 457-459, verbatim match) is the GENERAL author-focus-indicator 3:1 requirement whose original context is the gray #AAA low-ratio Fail figure. The mechanism here is OCCLUSION, not a low ratio (navy ~13:1 standalone). The .md's primary citation, F78.html lines 56-58, is the precise on-point quote ('focus indicator drawn just outside the border, but as both are black and the border is thicker... it no longer meets the definition of visible') and matches verbatim. Both citations are accurate; the F78 one is the load-bearing one.

The inspect.js tool's `input:focus` resolved to #memo (tool tab-focuses), not the autofocus target #amount documented in the scenario. Immaterial: both are identical text inputs (3px navy border, 1px same-navy outline, offset 0), so the F78(b) occlusion holds for the documented focused element.

Not a defect, but a labeling note: the .md 'Citation' section lists F78 (failures/F78.html) as the primary reference and the Understanding non-text-contrast.html quote second, whereas the prompt names the Understanding quote as the claimed citation. Both quotes are verbatim and on-point, so this is only an ordering/emphasis discrepancy, not a hallucination.

Minor signal artifact (does not affect verdict): the inspect tool's '.card:focus-visible' selector resolved to the FIRST card (112 Larkspur Ln, href #l1) rather than the autofocused 8 Meadowgate Ct card, because the tool emulates the focus-visible state across cards. The authored focus styling (outline rgb(27,58,43) solid 3px + halo box-shadow) is confirmed regardless.

Minor (not a defect): selector '.transfer-panel input' matches 4 inputs; inspect.js resolves only the first (#payee). All four share identical styling (white bg, 1px #3E5168 border on #003366 panel), so the per-edge=1.55:1 / interior-vs-panel=12.6:1 analysis applies uniformly to each — no inconsistency.

Note on label semantics: this is a PASS case, so 'errorIsReal' refers to the documented phenomenon (automated per-edge checkers wrongly FAIL it at 1.55:1) being genuine — confirmed real. The conformance verdict itself is correctly PASS.

Minor: the secondary failing element is input[type=date] (#dob). A native date input has UA-rendered internal chrome (spinbutton segments + calendar-picker affordance) that arguably provides a control-identification cue partly independent of the fill, making it a slightly less clean 1.4.11 case than the text input. The primary selector match (City or town text input) is unambiguous, so the case stands; strongest framing would lean on the text input alone.

Cosmetic only: font-family lists 'Public Sans' which is not bundled and falls back to Helvetica/Arial. No effect on rendering or the contrast verdict (failure is purely background-fill color, not text).
No defect: this is a deliberate boundary PASS case. There is no accessibility error to find — the documented expected outcome is 'passed', which is correct.

Minor framing caveat (not outcome-affecting): the 'why automated tools miss it' rationale targets a HYPOTHETICAL per-edge box-shadow contrast walker. Mainstream shipping checkers (axe-core, WAVE, Lighthouse) do not evaluate box-shadow bevel rings for SC 1.4.11 at all, so they would not actually produce the over-report the doc describes. The PASS verdict and the subsumption pedagogy remain valid, but the tool-failure narrative is aspirational rather than demonstrable against real tools.

Minor doc/CSS comment inconsistency for input B: CSS line 56 and md line 12 both cite border-vs-panel as 5.14:1, but the WHY comment block at HTML line 113 mistakenly says input A's border-vs-panel is 2.61:1 and at line 117 describes B correctly — this is cosmetic only and does not affect the element under test (input A). No effect on the FAIL verdict.

The 'nearly invisible' framing for input A is slightly strong: at 1.29:1 the white field is barely distinguishable from the lavender panel, but it is the below-3:1 border-vs-panel (2.61:1) that makes it a definite FAIL. Reasoning is still sound.

Interpretive tension (does NOT invalidate the case, but is the crux): the .pill.bad buttons DO contain clearly legible high-contrast text (#2A2F36 on #F4F6F8). The cited Understanding carve-out exempts a boundary from the SC when the control has 'visible content (such as text...) which helps users identify the presence of the control.' A strict reviewer could argue the legible text IS such content, making the outline NOT required and flipping the verdict to passed/inapplicable. The page's counter-argument (plain text with no interactive styling and fill==page does not by itself signal a *control* is present, so the outline remains the sole 'control here' cue) is defensible but contestable. This is precisely the human-judgment call the corpus targets, so it is a strength, not a defect.

Cosmetic: CSS sets border 1.5px but getComputedStyle reports '1px solid' (sub-pixel rounding). Width is irrelevant to non-text contrast; the border COLOR (#8E9BA6 = rgb(142,155,166)) is reported exactly, so this does not affect the verdict.

Minor reasoning inaccuracy (does NOT change verdict): the page comments (html lines 121-122) and md (lines 9, 36-38) claim the border #3A4658 is 'closest in brightness to the near-black surroundings' and 'subsumed into the dark background' (panel). By actual relative luminance the border (L=0.0598) is marginally CLOSER to the interior fill #1B2230 (L=0.0159, diff 0.044) than to the panel #11151C (L=0.0074, diff 0.052). The border is the brightest of the three elements. The WCAG rule says a border is subsumed into the color closest in brightness, which here is the interior, not the panel — so the stated subsumption-direction rationale is slightly off. The FAIL still holds robustly because EVERY adjacency is < 3:1 (interior-vs-panel 1.15, border-vs-panel 1.91, border-vs-interior 1.67), so no identifying cue reaches 3:1 under any subsumption reading.
Secondary defect not under test: input has 'outline: none' (html line 58) suppressing the UA focus indicator — a 2.4.7 Focus Visible concern, out of scope for this 1.4.11 case but worth noting.

Detectability nuance: because all three adjacencies are below 3:1, even an aggressive automated checker measuring interior-vs-panel would surface A failure here; the human judgment is needed to identify the CORRECT cue/reason (which element governs), not strictly to detect that a failure exists.

Directory name 'focus-indicator-geometry-inner-border-partly-outside' mislabels the mechanism: the actual implementation is a pure box-shadow:inset ring drawn ENTIRELY inside the component (the 'only inside the component' case, Understanding list item line 124), NOT the 'partly inside and partly outside' case (line 126). The .html, .md, citation and contrast math are all internally consistent on the correct 'only inside' mechanism, so this is a cosmetic naming defect, not a substantive one — but the folder name should be corrected to avoid implying the line-126 geometry (which has a DIFFERENT and more lenient rule: 'either part of the indicator can contrast').

The selector '#btn-confirm:focus' is not directly queryable by the inspect tool (reports 'selector not found' for pseudo-class selectors); the focus styling was instead confirmed via the tool's tabOrder boxShadow signals. Not a page defect, just a verification note.

Folder naming mismatch: the directory is named 'focus-indicator-geometry-inner-border-partly-outside' but case-02 is about a fully OUTER outline (outline-offset:4px) that must beat the page — it is the figure-focus-outer-yellow/green example, not the 'partly inside/partly outside' geometry. Cosmetic taxonomy error, does not affect the verdict.

Copy inconsistency: the .html help text (line 74) and the .md (line 8) call the controls 'links', but they are <button> elements (AX tree confirms role=button for both). Cosmetic only; no effect on the SC 1.4.11 verdict.

Prompt 'Claimed scenario' is stale/wrong: it describes a 'Lumen Photo Cloud pricing page', a 'ghost button' with a 'light blue-tinted interior', and selector #cta-pro:focus. The actual page is a Cedar Park Health appointment-confirmation page with a SOLID-blue primary button #confirm. This is a prompt-metadata mismatch only; the .html and .md are internally consistent and correct (solid-blue button, #confirm:focus, blue #4189B9 interior). The page itself is sound.

inspect.js reports selector '#confirm:focus' = 'selector not found' because :focus is a dynamic pseudo-class the static querySelector resolver cannot match. This is a tool limitation, not a page defect — the tab-order walk captured the authoritative focused state (stops 18/20/23: outlineStyle none, border 2px solid rgb(75,147,58)=#4B933A).

No defects found. This is a correctly-constructed PASS boundary case (expected outcome = passed), not a failure case; 'errorIsReal' is interpreted as 'the documented scenario/mechanism genuinely exists and the outcome label is correct', which it does.

Minor (non-blocking): the .seat:focus boxShadow uses two equal 2px layers with the same spread, so the inset and outset halves render as a single contiguous 4px band rather than a visually segmented half-in/half-out ring. The geometry is still correct (CSS box-shadow inset draws inside the border box, non-inset draws outside), so the 'straddling' claim holds, but the inner/outer separation is conceptual, not visibly distinct. Does not change the verdict.

Cataloging/scenario-name mismatch: the parent directory is named 'focus-indicator-geometry-inner-border-partly-outside' (implying an inset/inner-border geometry that is partly outside), but case-05 uses a pure OUTER ring 'box-shadow:0 0 0 3px <grey>' with no inset. The case's own .md/.html are internally consistent (they explicitly describe an outer ring on white), so this is a directory-name mismatch only, not an accessibility defect.

Tooling nuance (not a page defect): the documented selector '#tool-export:focus' returns 'selector not found' in inspect.js's static querySelector path because ':focus' is a dynamic pseudo-class; the failing ring is only observable in the tab-order walk, where the export button correctly resolves to boxShadow rgb(170,170,170). A reviewer testing the literal selector statically must apply focus first.

Cosmetic/non-blocking: the containing directory is named 'focus-indicator-geometry-inner-border-partly-outside' but this case is a fully-INSIDE (inset) indicator, not partly-outside. Verified the folder is a thematic umbrella covering multiple geometry subtypes (case-04 straddles the boundary, case-05 is an outer ring), so the directory name is a grouping label, not a per-case claim. case-06's own HTML and .md are internally consistent on the inner-border subtype, so this is not a defect in the case itself.

Minor internal numerical inconsistency: the .note prose (lines 99-100) states the border is '~1.46:1 on white', while the CSS comment (lines 33,37), the inline CSS note, and the .md doc all say '~1.66:1'. The actual computed WCAG ratio for #c9c9c9 on #ffffff is 1.6559:1, so the .note value of 1.46 is wrong (cosmetic prose only; does not affect the verdict since both are well under 3:1).

Directory name 'exemption-boundaries-inactive-hover-essential-symbolic' references hover/essential/symbolic mechanisms that are not present in this case (no :hover state change, no essential/symbolic content). This appears to be a shared bucket folder name rather than a per-case descriptor; case-01 only exercises the active-vs-disabled exemption-boundary mechanism.

The label text #8a8a8a vs white computes to 3.45:1 (above 3:1 but below the 4.5:1 of 1.4.3). This does not weaken the 1.4.11 claim, but the doc's framing that the faint label alone cannot identify a control is a judgment call rather than a hard threshold; the border is nonetheless the primary control-identifying boundary and it fails.

The page is a PASS case by design — there is no real accessibility issue, which is correct and intended. errorIsReal=false reflects that there is no genuine SC 1.4.11 violation (this is the intended outcome, not a defect).

Minor realism overstatement: the .md/.html narrative claims 'a scanner sampling :hover would flag a 1.4.11 failure.' No mainstream automated checker (axe-core has no 1.4.11 non-text-contrast rule at all; WAVE/Lighthouse do not synthetically trigger :hover and sample backgrounds for non-text contrast) actually produces this false positive. The false-positive premise is hypothetical rather than reflecting a real shipping tool's behavior. The PASS verdict itself is still correct.

The directory name references 'inactive' — the first checkbox (#essential) is disabled, which is independently exempt from 1.4.11; this is consistent and does not affect the verdict, but the case's discriminating mechanism is really the supplemental-hover exemption, not the disabled state.

Live-text caveat weakens the 'automated tools miss it' framing: the nine wordmarks are real text (color:#1c1c1c on #000, computed 1.232:1), so a generic text-contrast scanner (axe-core/Lighthouse/WAVE at the 1.4.3 layer) WOULD already surface a low-contrast violation on all ten elements. The .md/legend claim that 'a scanner sees ten low-contrast elements and cannot tell ... most contrast tools would either exempt all logo-like elements or flag all ten identically' is the accurate part; but the page is not a 'scanner sees nothing' case. The genuinely human-only judgment is the 1.4.11 EXEMPTION split (brand-mandated navy = NA vs author-choice near-black = FAIL), which no checker can derive.

Minor SC-boundary nuance: because the elements are live text rather than images, a purist could argue text contrast belongs to 1.4.3 (Contrast Minimum) rather than 1.4.11 (Non-text Contrast). This is NOT a defect, however — the WCAG 2.2 Understanding doc for 1.4.11 explicitly authors this exact 'logos low-contrast by author choice, white on hover' scenario in its 'Logos' section (lines 659-673) and the canonical figure 1.4.11-ntc-author-choice-logos.png, so labeling it 1.4.11 follows WCAG's own normative framing. Worth noting only so reviewers know the page is deliberately modeled on that figure.

Hover/focus reveal (.logo:hover,.logo:focus-visible{color:#fff}, line 37) does NOT rescue the failure — the resting/default state is the tested state (1.232:1) and the same Understanding doc's Dynamic Examples section states the unfocused default must already have sufficient contrast. Correctly handled by the case; documented to confirm I checked the reveal does not invalidate the FAIL.

Minor (non-blocking): the dialog is role="dialog" but non-modal with no JS handlers and no focus management; buttons are inert mocks. Acceptable for a pure contrast fixture but slightly weakens the 'trapped in the dialog' framing in the .md.
The .md gives ratios as ~1.4 and ~6.6; precise computed values are 1.434 and 6.57 — close enough, no defect.

Citation for the Essential-exception quote uses an ellipsis ('...') to stitch two non-adjacent (but consecutive list-item) sentences from the reference; both fragments ARE verbatim at lines 734-735 of wcag-understanding/non-text-contrast.html and both support the NA claim, so this is acceptable but worth noting that it is a join of two list items rather than one contiguous sentence.

Minor: the .md describes the adjacent area as '#e9eef1/#fbf7ef', but the button center (~201,131) sits inside the vitreous ellipse (#fbf7ef) and possibly over the heat-map path; the precise adjacent color is ambiguous. Not a defect: the ring fails 3:1 against ALL plausible adjacent colors (1.57:1 vs #e9eef1, 1.72:1 vs #fbf7ef, 1.0-2.4:1 vs heat-map stops, max 1.84:1 vs pure white), so the failure verdict is robust regardless.

Minor code-comment inaccuracy (cosmetic, does not affect verdict): CSS line 52 comment says the close glyph is '✕ at ~2.0:1 on #fff bar' and the .md/CSS repeatedly say ~2.0:1, but #9c9c9c on #ffffff computes to 2.75:1 (and 2.63:1 on the #fafafa page bg). The task prompt's ~2.75:1 is the correct figure. Either way it is below 3:1, so the FAIL verdict stands.
Doc rounds the faint icon to ~1.7:1; actual #b9b9b9 on #e7e7e7 is 1.59:1 (prompt's ~1.6:1 is closer). Below 3:1 regardless — no impact on verdict.
Doc says Zoom icon is ~7.6:1; #3a3a3a on #e7e7e7 actually computes to 9.20:1. Still well above 3:1, so the NA boundary is correct; only the cited ratio is off.

Edge-case for the close glyph: because it is an actual text character (✕) rendered at ~1.45rem, a text-contrast (1.4.3) checker could flag it as large-text below 3:1, so that one element is partially lint-reachable; however its classification as symbolic NON-TEXT content under 1.4.11 (vs language text) still requires human reasoning.
